# 12-Week Postpartum Return-to-Movement Programme

### Client Profile
**Age:** 33 | **Status:** 4 weeks post uncomplicated C-section | **Clearance:** Light activity only until 6-week OB check | **Equipment:** Yoga mat, home setting | **Goal:** Safe, progressive return to functional movement and core integrity

---

## Important Programme Notes for the Trainer

Before beginning, please review these standing guidelines with your client and revisit them at every session or check-in.

**C-section specific considerations:** The abdominal wall has been cut through multiple layers — skin, fascia, and uterus. Even with OB clearance at six weeks, internal healing continues for up to twelve months. This programme treats the scar and surrounding tissue with respect throughout all twelve weeks. There is no "powering through" here.

**The traffic light rule:** Teach your client to self-monitor using three signals. Green means she feels comfortable and in control. Amber means she notices pressure, pulling, or fatigue — she modifies or stops. Red means pain, leaking urine, heaviness in the pelvic floor, or doming/coning of the abdomen — she stops immediately and you are notified before the next session.

**Diastasis recti awareness:** Do not programme traditional crunches, sit-ups, double-leg lowers, or any exercise that causes visible coning or doming along the midline at any point in this twelve weeks. If you observe or she reports this, refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist before progressing.

**Pelvic floor physiotherapist referral:** Strongly recommend she sees a pelvic floor physio at or just after her six-week check, regardless of how well she feels. This is best practice, not a sign that something is wrong.

**Sleep and recovery context:** She is four weeks postpartum. Sleep deprivation is real and affects recovery, hormonal state, and tissue repair. Sessions should leave her feeling better than when she started, never depleted.

---

## Programme Architecture

| Phase | Weeks | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1: Reconnect | 1–2 (Programme weeks, i.e. weeks 4–6 post-birth) | Breath, pelvic floor, gentle mobility — pre-clearance safe |
| Phase 2: Rebuild Foundation | 3–6 (Post OB clearance) | Deep core activation, postural restoration, scar mobility |
| Phase 3: Restore Function | 7–10 | Loaded movement patterns, strength endurance, daily function |
| Phase 4: Progress and Integrate | 11–12 | Progressive loading, movement confidence, next-phase readiness |

---

---

# PHASE 1 — RECONNECT
## Weeks 1–2 of Programme (Weeks 4–6 Post C-Section)

### Phase Goals
Restore the neurological connection to the deep core and pelvic floor. Reduce post-surgical tension and stiffness. Establish breathing mechanics that support healing. Build a sustainable daily movement habit without overloading healing tissue.

### Session Structure
**Frequency:** Once daily, 10–15 minutes. These are not "workouts" in the traditional sense — frame them to your client as healing sessions. There is no intensity here, only awareness and gentleness.

**Format:** All sessions follow the same gentle flow during these two weeks. Variety comes from progressing breath and pelvic floor work, not from adding new exercises.

---

### The Daily Healing Session — Weeks 1 and 2

**Opening: Diaphragmatic Breathing — 3–5 minutes**

Have your client lie on her back with knees bent, feet flat, a pillow under her head if needed for comfort. Place one hand on her chest and one on her lower ribs. The goal is to breathe so that the lower hand rises and the chest hand stays relatively still. Inhale for a count of four, feeling the ribcage expand in all directions — front, sides, and back into the mat. Exhale slowly for a count of six, allowing everything to soften. This is the foundation of every phase that follows. The exhale is where pelvic floor engagement will eventually be layered in, so getting the breath pattern right now is non-negotiable.

Do this for ten to fifteen breath cycles before moving on.

**Pelvic Floor Reconnection — 5 minutes**

Remaining in the same position, introduce pelvic floor awareness. Many women post C-section assume their pelvic floor is fine because the birth was surgical, but the pelvic floor has carried the weight of pregnancy for nine months and is affected by hormonal changes, posture, and the surgery itself. The goal in weeks one and two is simply reconnection, not strength.

*Gentle lift and release:* On the exhale, ask her to imagine gently picking up a blueberry with her pelvic floor — a small, soft lift inward and upward. Hold for two to three seconds, then fully release on the inhale. The release is as important as the lift. Repeat eight to ten times. If she cannot feel anything, that is normal and not alarming — the connection will return. If she feels pain, stop.

*Pelvic floor breathing:* On the inhale, she consciously allows the pelvic floor to soften and descend slightly. On the exhale, it gently lifts. This coordinates the diaphragm and pelvic floor as a pressure management system, which is the foundation of all core work to come.

**Gentle Mobility — 5 minutes**

*Knee rolls (supine):* Lying on her back, knees bent together, she slowly lets both knees fall to one side, only as far as is comfortable with no pulling at the scar. Return to centre and repeat to the other side. Eight repetitions each side. This is not a stretch — it is a gentle invitation to movement.

*Ankle circles and foot pumps:* Simple ankle mobility to support circulation. Ten circles each direction, ten pumps. This is particularly relevant post-surgery for circulation.

*Supported cat-cow on hands and knees (Week 2 only, if comfortable):* Moving onto hands and knees, she gently rounds the back on the exhale and allows it to soften into a gentle arch on the inhale. The range of motion is very small — this is not a full yoga cat-cow. Watch for any pulling or discomfort at the scar site. If hands and knees is uncomfortable, skip this until Phase 2.

**Closing: Walking**

Walking is her primary cardiovascular and functional activity in Phase 1. Begin with ten minutes daily in week one, building to fifteen to twenty minutes by the end of week two. Flat terrain, comfortable pace, supportive footwear. She should be able to hold a conversation throughout. If she experiences pelvic heaviness, leaking, or scar pain, she shortens the walk and you note it.

---

### Trainer Check-In Points — End of Week 2

Before progressing to Phase 2, confirm the following. She has received her six-week OB clearance. She can perform ten pelvic floor lifts with conscious control and full release. She has no pain during or after the daily sessions. She is walking twenty minutes comfortably. If any of these are not met, extend Phase 1 by one week and reassess.

---
---

# PHASE 2 — REBUILD FOUNDATION
## Weeks 3–6 of Programme (Weeks 6–10 Post C-Section)

### Phase Goals
With OB clearance now in place, begin activating the deep core system — specifically the transversus abdominis — in a controlled, pressure-managed way. Introduce scar tissue mobility work. Restore hip and thoracic mobility. Begin gentle lower body loading through bodyweight patterns. Continue building walking duration and confidence.

### Session Structure
**Frequency:** 3 sessions per week with at least one rest day between sessions. Walking continues on non-session days.

**Session length:** 20–30 minutes.

**Session format:** Breath and pelvic floor warm-up (5 minutes) → Main work (15–20 minutes) → Closing mobility or relaxation (5 minutes).

---

### Scar Tissue Mobility — Introduce at Week 3

This is one of the most important and most overlooked components of C-section recovery. Scar tissue can adhere to underlying fascia and affect movement, posture, bladder function, and even future pregnancies. Introduce this gently and only once the scar is fully closed with no scabbing.

*Desensitisation (Week 3):* Using a soft cloth or her fingertips, she gently touches the skin around the scar — not on it — in different textures and pressures. Many women find the area numb or hypersensitive. This is normal. Spend two to three minutes daily doing this.

*Skin rolling above the scar (Week 4 onwards):* Once she is comfortable with touch around the scar, she can begin gently picking up the skin just above the scar line between thumb and forefinger and rolling it slowly. This mobilises the superficial fascia. She should feel a mild pulling sensation but no pain. One to two minutes daily.

*Direct scar massage (Week 6 onwards, if scar is well healed):* Using two fingers, she applies gentle downward pressure directly on the scar and moves the skin in small circles — up, down, and side to side. The goal is to prevent the scar from adhering to deeper layers. Two to three minutes daily. If she notices any pulling into the bladder or bowel, refer to pelvic floor physio.

---

### Week 3 Sessions

**Session A**

*Diaphragmatic breathing with transversus abdominis connection — 3 sets of 8 breaths*
Building on Phase 1, add a new layer. On the exhale, as the pelvic floor gently lifts, she also draws the lower abdomen very gently inward — imagine the hip bones softly moving toward each other. This is a 20–30% contraction, not a bracing or sucking in. Hold for the length of the exhale, release fully on the inhale. This is the foundation of all core work in this programme.

*Supine heel slides — 3 sets of 8 per side*
Lying on her back, knees bent. On the exhale with pelvic floor and gentle TA engaged, she slowly slides one heel along the mat until the leg is straight, then slides it back. The lower back stays in neutral — no arching. If she feels any doming at the midline or pressure in the scar, she reduces range of motion. This is the first true core challenge of the programme.

*Glute bridges — 3 sets of 10*
Lying on her back, knees bent, feet hip-width apart. On the exhale, she engages the pelvic floor and gently lifts the hips to a comfortable height — not forcing a full bridge. Hold for two seconds at the top, lower slowly. This restores posterior chain activation and addresses the anterior pelvic tilt common in postpartum women. Watch that she is not gripping her glutes aggressively or holding her breath.

*Supported side-lying hip abduction — 2 sets of 10 per side*
Lying on her side with knees slightly bent, she lifts the top leg to hip height and lowers slowly. Keep the movement controlled and the pelvis stacked. This begins reactivating the hip abductors and lateral stabilisers without any load through the scar.

*Thoracic rotation in side-lying — 2 sets of 8 per side*
Lying on her side with knees bent and stacked, arms extended in front. She slowly opens the top arm toward the ceiling and behind her, following with her eyes, then returns. The lower body stays still. This addresses the thoracic stiffness that comes from feeding posture and carrying a baby.

**Session B**

*Breathing warm-up — 5 minutes as established*

*Four-point kneeling opposite arm and leg reach — 3 sets of 8 per side*
On hands and knees, spine in neutral. On the exhale with gentle core engagement, she extends one arm forward and the opposite leg back to hip height. Hold for three seconds, return with control. This is a low-load anti-rotation and stability exercise. Watch for any rotation in the pelvis or ribcage flare.

*Clamshells — 3 sets of 12 per side*
Side-lying, hips stacked, knees bent at approximately 45 degrees. She opens the top knee like a clamshell while keeping the feet together and the pelvis still. Slow and controlled. This targets the hip external rotators and glute medius, which are important for pelvic stability.

*Wall push-up — 3 sets of 10*
Standing facing a wall, hands at shoulder height and width. She performs a controlled push-up against the wall, maintaining a straight body line and breathing throughout. This begins upper body and shoulder girdle work without any load through the abdomen.

*Standing hip hinge — 3 sets of 10*
Standing with feet hip-width apart, she places her hands on her hips and hinges forward from the hips — not the waist — until she feels a gentle stretch in the hamstrings, then returns to standing. This teaches the hip hinge pattern that will underpin all lower body loading in later phases. Keep the spine long and neutral throughout.

**Session C**

*Breathing warm-up — 5 minutes*

*Repeat Session A exercises with one additional set each*

*Add: Seated posture work — 5 minutes*
Sitting cross-legged or in a chair, she works on stacking her ribcage over her pelvis, drawing the shoulder blades gently together and down, and lengthening through the crown of the head. This directly addresses the forward head posture and rounded shoulders that develop during feeding and carrying. She can practise this while feeding the baby.

---

### Weeks 4–6 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 2

Progress the following variables across weeks four, five, and six. Do not progress all variables simultaneously — choose one per session.

**Heel slides:** Progress from single leg to adding a brief hold at full extension (three to five seconds) before returning.

**Glute bridges:** Progress to a three-second hold at the top, then to a single-leg bridge with the non-working leg extended (only if no doming or scar discomfort).

**Four-point reach:** Increase hold time to five seconds, then add a slow three-count return.

**Walking:** Build to thirty minutes on non-session days by the end of week six. Introduce gentle inclines if available and comfortable.

**Add in Week 5 — Supported squat:**
Standing with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out, she holds a door frame or the back of a sturdy chair for support. She slowly lowers into a squat to a comfortable depth — initially this may be only a quarter squat — and returns to standing. Three sets of ten. Focus is on the pattern, not the depth. Exhale on the way up with pelvic floor engagement.

**Add in Week 6 — Step-ups onto a low step or stair:**
Using the bottom stair, she steps up with one foot, brings the other foot up, then steps back down with control. Three sets of ten per side. This introduces single-leg loading and functional movement. Hold the wall for balance if needed.

---

### Trainer Check-In Points — End of Week 6

She should be able to perform all Phase 2 exercises without doming, leaking, or pain. She should have seen a pelvic floor physiotherapist by this point if at all possible. She should be walking thirty minutes comfortably. She should feel the connection between her breath, pelvic floor, and deep core during movement. If she has not seen a pelvic floor physio, make this a priority before Phase 3.

---
---

# PHASE 3 — RESTORE FUNCTION
## Weeks 7–10 of Programme (Weeks 10–14 Post C-Section)

### Phase Goals
Introduce functional movement patterns with progressive bodyweight loading. Build strength endurance in the lower body, posterior chain, and shoulder girdle. Increase session duration and complexity. Develop the capacity to manage the physical demands of daily life with a baby — carrying, lifting from the floor, standing for extended periods.

### Session Structure
**Frequency:** 3–4 sessions per week.

**Session length:** 30–40 minutes.

**Format:** Dynamic warm-up (5–8 minutes) → Main circuit or superset work (20–25 minutes) → Cool-down and mobility (5–7 minutes).

---

### Dynamic Warm-Up — Used Throughout Phase 3

This replaces the purely supine breathing warm-up, though she should still begin with three to five diaphragmatic breaths to connect to her core before moving.

- Marching on the spot with arm swings — 30 seconds
- Hip circles standing — 10 each direction
- Leg swings front to back — 10 each leg
- Leg swings side to side — 10 each leg
- Thoracic rotation standing — 8 each side
- Shallow squat with hold — 5 repetitions, 3-second hold at bottom

---

### Week 7 Sessions

**Session A — Lower Body and Core**

*Bodyweight squat — 3 sets of 12*
Full bodyweight squat now, progressing from the supported version. Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out, chest tall, exhale on the way up with pelvic floor engagement. If she experiences any pelvic heaviness or leaking, return to the supported version and refer to pelvic floor physio.

*Reverse lunge — 3 sets of 10 per side*
Standing, she steps one foot back and lowers the back knee toward the mat, keeping the front shin vertical. Return to standing. This is preferable to a forward lunge at this stage as it places less demand on the pelvic floor. Exhale on the return to standing.

*Glute bridge with march — 3 sets of 8 per side*
In the bridge position at the top, she slowly lifts one foot off the mat, holds for two seconds, replaces it, then lifts the other. The pelvis must stay level throughout. This is a significant progression from the standard bridge.

*Dead bug — 3 sets of 6 per side*
Lying on her back, arms pointing to the ceiling, knees bent at 90 degrees in the air (tabletop position). On the exhale with core engaged, she slowly lowers one arm overhead and the opposite leg toward the mat — only as far as she can maintain a neutral spine and no doming. Return on the inhale. This is the first true anti-extension core exercise in the programme and should be introduced carefully. If she cannot maintain neutral spine or if doming occurs, regress to heel slides.

*Side-lying hip abduction with straight leg — 3 sets of 12 per side*
Progressing from the bent-knee version in Phase 2.

**Session B — Upper Body and Posture**

*Wall push-up progressed to incline push-up — 3 sets of 10*
Using the mat against a low surface such as a sofa or coffee table, she performs a push-up at a lower angle than the wall version. If this is comfortable, she can progress to a full mat push-up on knees by week eight.

*Prone Y-T-W — 2 sets of 8 each shape*
Lying face down on the mat, she lifts her arms into a Y shape (overhead), then a T shape (out to the sides), then a W shape (elbows bent, hands by ears). Each position is held for two seconds. This targets the lower and mid trapezius and is excellent for the postural issues that develop from feeding and carrying. Keep the neck long and the forehead resting on a folded towel if needed.

*Four-point kneeling row simulation — 3 sets of 10 per side*
On hands and knees, she lifts one hand off the mat, bends the elbow, and draws it back as if rowing. Hold for two seconds, lower with control. This builds single-arm stability and upper back strength.

*Standing shoulder external rotation — 3 sets of 12 per side*
Standing with one elbow bent at 90 degrees and tucked to her side, she rotates the forearm outward. Without a resistance band this is a movement pattern drill — she can add a resistance band when available, but for now the focus is on the movement and the mind-muscle connection.

*Thoracic extension over a rolled mat — 2 sets of 8 breaths*
Rolling the yoga mat into a firm cylinder, she places it horizontally across her mid-back and gently extends over it, arms crossed over the chest. This is a passive thoracic mobility exercise that counteracts the flexion-dominant posture of new motherhood. Hold each extension for a full breath cycle.

**Session C — Full Body Circuit**

Perform as a circuit with 45 seconds of work and 15 seconds of transition. Complete three rounds with two minutes of rest between rounds.

- Bodyweight squat
- Reverse lunge alternating legs
- Incline or knee push-up
- Glute bridge
- Four-point opposite arm and leg reach
- Standing hip hinge
- Side-lying hip abduction (switch sides each round)
- Dead bug (slow and controlled — quality over quantity)

---

### Weeks 8–10 — Progressive Overload Within Phase 3

**Week 8 progressions:**
- Squat: Add a two-second pause at the bottom.
- Reverse lunge: Increase to 12 repetitions per side.
- Dead bug: Increase to 8 repetitions per side.
- Push-up: Progress to knee push-up on the mat if not already there.
- Add: Sumo squat — feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out more, same breathing and pelvic floor cues. Three sets of twelve.

**Week 9 progressions:**
- Introduce the Romanian deadlift pattern: Standing, hinging at the hip with a long spine, she reaches both hands toward the mat as far as she can while maintaining neutral spine, then returns to standing. Three sets of ten. This is the foundation for eventually loading with a kettlebell or dumbbell in future programming.
- Glute bridge: Progress to single-leg glute bridge — one foot flat, one leg extended. Three sets of eight per side.
- Push-up: Progress to full push-up on the mat if knee push-up is comfortable and there is no doming.
- Walking: Introduce one longer walk per week of forty to forty-five minutes.

**Week 10 progressions:**
- Squat: Add a slow three-count descent.
- Reverse lunge: Progress to a walking lunge across the mat.
- Dead bug: Progress to a longer hold — five seconds at the extended position.
- Add: Step-up with knee drive — stepping up onto the stair and driving the back knee up to hip height before stepping down. Three sets of ten per side.
- Circuit day: Increase to four rounds.

---

### Trainer Check-In Points — End of Week 10

She should be performing all exercises with good form, appropriate breathing, and no symptoms. She should feel strong and capable in daily functional movements. She should have no leaking, prolapse symptoms, or scar discomfort during exercise. If she has not yet seen a pelvic floor physio, this is now urgent before Phase 4. She should be walking forty-five minutes comfortably and feeling ready for more challenge.

---
---

# PHASE 4 — PROGRESS AND INTEGRATE
## Weeks 11–12 of Programme (Weeks 14–16 Post C-Section)

### Phase Goals
Consolidate all gains from the previous three phases. Introduce more complex movement combinations and increase training density. Prepare her physically and psychologically for the next chapter of her fitness journey — whether that is returning to a gym, a group class, running, or continuing home training with added load. Leave her feeling capable, strong, and informed.

### Session Structure
**Frequency:** 4 sessions per week.

**Session length:** 35–45 minutes.

**Format:** Dynamic warm-up (5–8 minutes) → Strength superset block (20–25 minutes) → Functional finisher (5–8 minutes) → Cool-down (5 minutes).

---

### Week 11 Sessions

**Session A — Lower Body Strength**

*Superset 1 — 3 rounds:*
- Bodyweight squat with slow three-count descent, 12 repetitions
- Single-leg glute bridge, 10 per side

*Superset 2 — 3 rounds:*
- Walking lunge, 10 per side
- Romanian deadlift pattern, 12 repetitions

*Superset 3 — 3 rounds:*
- Step-up with knee drive, 10 per side
- Side-lying hip abduction, 15 per side

*Functional finisher — 5 minutes:*
Floor-to-stand practice. She starts standing, lowers herself to the mat in a controlled way using whatever pattern feels natural, then returns to standing. She practises this ten times, exploring different ways to get up and down from the floor — this is one of the most functional skills for a parent of a young child. Encourage her to notice which patterns feel strong and which feel effortful.

**Session B — Upper Body and Core**

*Superset 1 — 3 rounds:*
- Full push-up or knee push-up, 10 repetitions
- Prone Y

# Nutrition Plan — Postpartum Breastfeeding Support
### Integrated with the 12-Week Return-to-Movement Programme

---

## Critical Framing Note for the Trainer

Before presenting any nutrition guidance to this client, establish the following clearly and compassionately. **This is not a fat loss plan.** Postpartum nutrition during breastfeeding has one primary job: support healing, support milk production, and support the energy demands of keeping a small human alive while also moving a body that is recovering from major abdominal surgery. Weight loss as a goal is explicitly off the table for this twelve-week period. If she raises it, acknowledge it, validate that the feeling is understandable, and redirect her firmly toward nourishment. Undereating while breastfeeding compromises milk supply, delays tissue healing, worsens postpartum mood, and increases injury risk during exercise. It is not a neutral choice.

You are not a registered dietitian. Present this plan as general evidence-informed guidance and recommend she also consults her GP, midwife, or a registered dietitian — particularly if she has any history of disordered eating, gestational diabetes, thyroid conditions, or iron deficiency anaemia, all of which are common in the postpartum period and all of which affect nutritional needs significantly.

---

## Caloric Needs — The Baseline

Breastfeeding requires approximately **400–500 additional calories per day** above her pre-pregnancy maintenance needs. This is not optional — it is the metabolic cost of milk production. For a 33-year-old woman of average height and weight who is lightly active and breastfeeding, total daily caloric needs will typically fall somewhere in the range of **2,000–2,400 calories per day**, though this varies considerably by body size, milk volume, and activity level.

As she progresses through the exercise programme and her activity level increases in Phases 3 and 4, her caloric needs will increase further. The principle throughout is simple: **eat enough to feel energised, produce milk, and recover from movement.** Hunger is a signal to eat, not a signal to resist.

If she is not breastfeeding, reduce the additional 400–500 calories but maintain all other nutritional principles below, as healing and exercise recovery demands remain the same.

---

## Macronutrient Framework

Rather than prescribing rigid gram targets, which are impractical for a sleep-deprived new mother, this plan uses a **plate-building model** that is flexible, intuitive, and does not require weighing or tracking food. Tracking apps are explicitly not recommended at this stage — the cognitive load is unnecessary and the focus on numbers can be counterproductive in the postpartum period.

---

### Protein — The Healing and Milk Macronutrient

**Target:** Approximately **1.5–1.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day.** For a woman of around 65–70 kg this means roughly 100–125 grams of protein daily. This is higher than standard recommendations because she is simultaneously healing surgical tissue, rebuilding muscle, and producing milk.

**Why it matters:** Protein provides the amino acids needed to repair the abdominal wall layers cut during the C-section, rebuild connective tissue and fascia, support the immune system, and maintain milk protein content. Inadequate protein intake is one of the most common nutritional gaps in postpartum women and directly affects recovery speed.

**Practical targets:** Aim for a meaningful protein source at every meal and at least one snack. A meaningful source means a portion that provides roughly 20–30 grams of protein.

**Best sources for this client:**

*Animal sources:* Eggs are the postpartum superfood — cheap, fast, versatile, and highly bioavailable. Two to three eggs provide approximately 18–24 grams of protein. Greek yoghurt provides 15–20 grams per 200g serving. Chicken, turkey, salmon, tuna, and sardines are all excellent. Salmon and sardines have the added benefit of providing omega-3 fatty acids, which are critical for infant brain development and maternal mood. Aim for two to three portions of oily fish per week, noting that she should avoid high-mercury fish such as swordfish, shark, and marlin while breastfeeding.

*Plant sources:* Lentils, chickpeas, black beans, and other legumes provide 15–18 grams per cooked cup and are also rich in iron and fibre. Tofu and tempeh are complete protein sources. Edamame is a fast, high-protein snack. Combine plant proteins across the day to ensure a full amino acid profile.

*Dairy:* Cottage cheese, hard cheeses, and milk all contribute meaningfully. Full-fat dairy is preferable at this stage — the fat supports fat-soluble vitamin absorption and provides caloric density without requiring large volumes of food.

---

### Carbohydrates — Energy, Mood, and Milk Supply

**Target:** Carbohydrates should make up approximately **40–50% of total calories.** This is not a low-carb plan. Carbohydrates are the brain's preferred fuel source, and a sleep-deprived, breastfeeding, healing woman needs her brain functioning as well as possible. Carbohydrate restriction has been associated with reduced milk supply and worsened postpartum mood. It is contraindicated here.

**Focus on quality and fibre:** The goal is not to avoid carbohydrates but to choose those that provide sustained energy, fibre, and micronutrients rather than rapid spikes and crashes.

**Best sources:**

*Whole grains:* Oats are particularly valuable — they are quick to prepare, high in fibre, provide beta-glucan which may support milk supply, and are rich in iron. Porridge with protein additions such as Greek yoghurt, nut butter, or seeds is an ideal postpartum breakfast. Brown rice, wholegrain bread, wholegrain pasta, and quinoa are all excellent staples.

*Root vegetables:* Sweet potato, regular potato, butternut squash, and parsnip provide carbohydrates alongside potassium, vitamin C, and fibre. Roasting a large batch at the start of the week makes these accessible without daily cooking effort.

*Fruit:* All fruit is appropriate. Bananas are particularly useful as a fast, one-handed snack that requires no preparation — relevant when she is holding a baby. Berries are rich in antioxidants that support tissue healing. Dried fruit such as dates, apricots, and figs provide concentrated energy and iron.

*Legumes:* Lentils, chickpeas, and beans count toward both protein and carbohydrate targets and are among the most nutritionally dense foods available.

---

### Fats — Hormones, Healing, and Infant Brain Development

**Target:** Approximately **30–35% of total calories** from fat, with a strong emphasis on quality.

**Why it matters:** Dietary fat directly influences the fatty acid composition of breast milk, particularly the omega-3 content which is critical for infant neurological development. Fat also supports the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K — all of which are important for healing and immune function. Hormonal recovery postpartum is also fat-dependent.

**Best sources:**

*Omega-3 rich:* Oily fish as above. Walnuts, flaxseeds, and chia seeds provide plant-based omega-3 (ALA), though conversion to the active forms DHA and EPA is limited. If she does not eat fish regularly, an algae-based DHA supplement is worth discussing with her GP.

*Monounsaturated:* Avocado, olive oil, and almonds. Avocado on toast with eggs is a nutritionally excellent, fast postpartum meal. A drizzle of olive oil on vegetables or in cooking adds caloric density without requiring extra food volume.

*Saturated fat in moderation:* Full-fat dairy, eggs, and some meat. These are not foods to avoid — they provide important nutrients and caloric density. The concern is excess, not inclusion.

*Minimise:* Ultra-processed foods high in trans fats and refined vegetable oils. Not because of moral judgement — convenience food is a survival tool for new parents — but because these provide calories without the micronutrients she needs for healing and milk production.

---

## Micronutrients — The Non-Negotiables

These are the nutrients most commonly depleted in postpartum women and most critical for her recovery and her baby's development. Each one warrants specific attention.

---

### Iron

**Why it is critical:** Blood loss during a C-section is typically higher than vaginal birth — often 500–1,000ml. Combined with the iron demands of pregnancy, many women arrive postpartum with depleted iron stores. Low iron causes fatigue, poor exercise recovery, impaired immune function, and worsened postpartum mood. It is one of the most common and most underdiagnosed postpartum issues.

**Signs to watch for:** Excessive fatigue beyond what sleep deprivation explains, breathlessness during light activity, heart palpitations, difficulty concentrating, pale inner eyelids. If she presents with these, encourage her to request a full blood count from her GP before progressing the exercise programme.

**Dietary sources:** Red meat two to three times per week is the most bioavailable source. Lamb, beef, and venison are all excellent. For those who eat less meat, lentils, fortified cereals, dark leafy greens, tofu, pumpkin seeds, and dried apricots all contribute. Pair plant-based iron sources with vitamin C — a squeeze of lemon on lentils, orange juice with fortified cereal, or tomatoes with spinach — to significantly enhance absorption. Avoid tea and coffee within an hour of iron-rich meals as tannins inhibit absorption.

**Supplementation:** If her GP confirms low ferritin or haemoglobin, iron supplementation will be recommended. This is common and should not be alarming.

---

### Calcium

**Why it is critical:** Breastfeeding draws calcium from maternal stores to meet infant needs. If dietary intake is insufficient, the body draws from bone. This is a temporary and reversible process, but adequate dietary calcium minimises bone density loss during the breastfeeding period.

**Target:** Approximately 1,000–1,300mg per day.

**Dietary sources:** Dairy remains the most concentrated and bioavailable source — a 200ml glass of milk provides approximately 240mg, a 150g pot of yoghurt provides approximately 200mg, and 30g of hard cheese provides approximately 220mg. For those who avoid dairy, fortified plant milks provide comparable amounts if she chooses fortified versions. Tinned sardines and salmon eaten with the bones are excellent non-dairy sources. Tofu set with calcium sulphate, kale, broccoli, almonds, and fortified foods all contribute.

**Note:** Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption — see below.

---

### Vitamin D

**Why it is critical:** Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common in the UK and Ireland, particularly in winter months. It is essential for calcium absorption, immune function, mood regulation, and muscle function. Breast milk is naturally low in vitamin D, meaning exclusively breastfed infants are at risk of deficiency regardless of maternal status — the NHS recommends all breastfed babies receive a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5–10 micrograms.

**For the mother:** The NHS recommends all adults consider a daily supplement of 10 micrograms (400 IU) throughout the year, and this is particularly important postpartum. Many postpartum women benefit from higher doses — discuss with her GP, especially if she has darker skin, limited sun exposure, or a history of deficiency.

**Dietary sources:** Oily fish, egg yolks, fortified foods, and mushrooms exposed to UV light all contribute, but dietary sources alone are rarely sufficient in northern climates.

---

### Omega-3 Fatty Acids (DHA)

**Why it is critical:** DHA is the primary structural fat in the infant brain and retina. It is transferred through breast milk, drawing on maternal stores. Maternal DHA status is also strongly associated with postpartum mood — low DHA is linked to increased risk of postpartum depression.

**Target:** At least 200–300mg DHA per day, ideally more.

**Dietary sources:** Two to three portions of oily fish per week — salmon, mackerel, sardines, anchovies, herring — will meet this target. If she does not eat fish, an algae-based DHA supplement (the original source from which fish obtain their DHA) is the most appropriate alternative.

---

### Iodine

**Why it is critical:** Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone production and infant brain development. It is transferred through breast milk and requirements increase significantly during breastfeeding. Iodine deficiency is more common than many people realise, particularly in those who avoid dairy and fish.

**Dietary sources:** Dairy products and white fish are the primary dietary sources in the UK. Seaweed contains iodine but in highly variable and sometimes excessive amounts — it is not a reliable source. If she avoids dairy and fish, discuss iodine supplementation with her GP or dietitian.

---

### Folate and B Vitamins

**Why it is critical:** Folate requirements remain elevated during breastfeeding. B vitamins support energy metabolism, nervous system function, and red blood cell production. B12 is particularly important for those who eat little or no animal products, as breast milk B12 content directly reflects maternal intake.

**Dietary sources:** Dark leafy greens, legumes, eggs, meat, fish, and fortified foods. Those following a plant-based diet should supplement B12 without exception.

---

### Zinc

**Why it is critical:** Zinc supports immune function, wound healing, and tissue repair — all directly relevant to C-section recovery. It is also transferred through breast milk.

**Dietary sources:** Red meat, shellfish (particularly oysters), pumpkin seeds, legumes, nuts, and wholegrains. Phytates in plant foods reduce zinc absorption, so plant-based eaters need higher dietary intake.

---

## Hydration — The Most Underestimated Factor

Breastfeeding increases fluid requirements significantly. Milk production requires water, and dehydration reduces milk volume, increases fatigue, worsens headaches, and impairs exercise recovery.

**Target:** Approximately **2.5–3 litres of total fluid per day**, increasing on days she exercises. This sounds like a lot but includes fluid from food as well as drinks.

**Practical strategy:** Keep a large water bottle — at least 750ml — within reach at all times, particularly during feeding sessions. Many women find they become intensely thirsty during let-down — this is a physiological signal and should be acted on immediately. Herbal teas count toward fluid intake. Coconut water is a useful electrolyte-containing option on exercise days.

**Caffeine:** She can consume caffeine while breastfeeding. Current guidance suggests up to 200mg per day is safe — approximately one to two cups of coffee or three to four cups of tea. Caffeine does pass into breast milk in small amounts and peaks approximately one to two hours after consumption. If her baby seems unsettled after she drinks coffee, she can time her caffeine intake immediately after a feed rather than before.

**Alcohol:** Outside the scope of this plan, but if she asks — current guidance recommends avoiding alcohol while breastfeeding or waiting at least two to three hours per unit before feeding.

---

## Supplementation Recommendations

The following supplements are appropriate to discuss with her GP or midwife. Many women continue their pregnancy multivitamin throughout breastfeeding, which is a reasonable approach, but the following specific supplements are worth highlighting.

**Continue or begin:**
- **Postnatal multivitamin** specifically formulated for breastfeeding — these typically contain appropriate levels of iodine, folate, iron, and B vitamins. Brands formulated for breastfeeding are preferable to standard pregnancy vitamins as the nutrient ratios differ.
- **Vitamin D — 10–25 micrograms (400–1,000 IU) daily** — discuss higher doses with GP if deficiency is suspected.
- **Omega-3 DHA — 200–500mg daily** — particularly if oily fish intake is less than two portions per week. Choose a product that specifies DHA content and is tested for heavy metals.

**Consider if indicated:**
- **Iron** — only if confirmed deficient by blood test. Self-supplementing iron without confirmed deficiency is not recommended.
- **Magnesium — 300mg daily** — not universally necessary but may support sleep quality, muscle recovery, and mood. Magnesium glycinate or citrate are the most bioavailable forms. Discuss with GP.
- **Probiotic** — emerging evidence suggests postnatal probiotic use may support maternal gut health and infant microbiome via breast milk. Not essential but reasonable to consider.

---

## Meal Timing and Structure

Rigid meal timing is not realistic for a new mother. The following framework is flexible and designed around the reality of her day.

---

### The Core Principle — Never Skip Meals, Never Let Hunger Become Urgent

Skipping meals while breastfeeding leads to blood sugar crashes, increased cortisol, reduced milk supply, and impaired mood and cognition. The goal is to eat regularly enough that she never reaches the point of desperate hunger. This requires preparation, not willpower.

---

### Meal Structure — Three Meals and Two to Three Snacks

**Breakfast — Within an Hour of Waking**

This is the most important meal of the day for a breastfeeding, healing woman. It sets blood sugar, provides morning energy, and contributes significantly to daily protein and micronutrient targets. It should be substantial, not token.

*Fast options (under five minutes):*
- Porridge made with full-fat milk, topped with a tablespoon of nut butter, a handful of berries, and a sprinkle of pumpkin seeds. Add a scoop of unflavoured protein powder if protein targets are difficult to meet.
- Greek yoghurt with granola, banana, and a drizzle of honey.
- Two to three scrambled eggs on wholegrain toast with half an avocado.
- Overnight oats prepared the night before — oats soaked in milk with chia seeds, topped with fruit and yoghurt in the morning.

**Mid-Morning Snack**

*Options:*
- A banana with a tablespoon of almond butter.
- A small handful of mixed nuts and a piece of fruit.
- Cottage cheese on oatcakes.
- A boiled egg prepared in advance with some cherry tomatoes.

**Lunch — Substantial and Protein-Led**

Lunch should be the second largest meal of the day. Batch cooking is the most practical strategy — preparing a large quantity of a base ingredient such as lentil soup, chicken and rice, or a bean stew at the start of the week means lunch requires only reheating.

*Options:*
- Lentil and vegetable soup with wholegrain bread and butter.
- Tinned salmon or sardines on wholegrain toast with salad.
- Leftover dinner from the night before — always cook extra.
- A large salad with chickpeas, feta, roasted vegetables, and olive oil dressing — prepare components in advance.
- Egg fried rice with frozen vegetables — fast, nutritious, and uses pantry staples.

**Afternoon Snack — Particularly Important on Exercise Days**

On days she exercises, this snack should ideally be consumed within thirty to sixty minutes after her session to support recovery. It should contain both protein and carbohydrate.

*Options:*
- Greek yoghurt with fruit.
- A smoothie — full-fat milk or fortified plant milk, banana, a handful of spinach, a tablespoon of nut butter, and optionally a scoop of protein powder.
- Wholegrain toast with peanut butter and sliced banana.
- Hummus with vegetable sticks and oatcakes.

**Dinner — Balanced and Varied**

Dinner should follow the plate model: roughly one quarter protein, one quarter complex carbohydrate, and one half vegetables, with a source of healthy fat included. The emphasis on vegetables is important for fibre, micronutrients, and gut health — but if she is struggling with appetite or time, a smaller plate of nutrient-dense food is better than a perfect plate she cannot manage.

*Weekly dinner rotation suggestions:*

*Monday:* Baked salmon with sweet potato and steamed broccoli. Drizzle with olive oil and lemon. This provides DHA, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and vitamin C in a single meal.

*Tuesday:* Chicken and vegetable stir-fry with brown rice. Use a variety of coloured vegetables — peppers, pak choi, carrots, sugar snap peas — for a broad micronutrient profile.

*Wednesday:* Red lentil dahl with brown rice or wholegrain naan and a side of wilted spinach. This is an iron-rich, high-fibre, high-protein plant-based meal that is also inexpensive and freezes well.

*Thursday:* Beef or lamb mince with roasted root vegetables and wholegrain pasta or potatoes. Red meat twice a week supports iron and zinc intake.

*Friday:* Egg and vegetable frittata with a large green salad. Fast, protein-rich, and uses whatever vegetables are in the fridge.

*Saturday:* Tinned sardine or mackerel fishcakes made with mashed potato, served with peas and a squeeze of lemon. Sardines eaten with bones provide calcium, DHA, and vitamin D.

*Sunday:* Batch cook day. A large pot of soup, a tray of roasted vegetables, a grain such as quinoa or brown rice, and a protein such as roasted chicken or a bean stew. These components form the basis of lunches and quick dinners for the week ahead.

**Evening Snack — Optional but Often Needed**

Breastfeeding women frequently experience hunger in the evening and overnight. This is physiological and should not be ignored. A small, protein-containing snack before bed supports overnight milk production and prevents blood sugar dropping during night feeds.

*Options:*
- A small bowl of Greek yoghurt with honey.
- Warm full-fat milk with a small handful of nuts.
- Wholegrain toast with nut butter.
- A small portion of leftover dinner.

---

## Batch Cooking and Practical Strategies

The most nutritious plan in the world is useless if it cannot be executed by a sleep-deprived woman with one free hand. The following strategies are non-negotiable practical tools.

**The Sunday reset:** Dedicate one to two hours on the weekend — with partner support if available — to preparing the week's food foundations. Cook a large grain, roast a tray of vegetables, prepare a batch of protein such as boiled eggs or cooked chicken, and make one large pot of soup or stew. This single investment dramatically reduces the daily cognitive and physical load of eating well.

**One-handed foods:** Stock the kitchen with foods that require no preparation and can be eaten with one hand during a feed. Bananas, dates, oatcakes, cheese portions, nuts, yoghurt pouches, and pre-cut fruit are all appropriate. These are not junk food — they are survival nutrition and should be treated as such.

**Freezer meals:** If she has support in the early weeks, encourage friends and family to bring freezer meals rather than flowers. Soups, stews, dahl, and casseroles all freeze well and provide nutritious meals on the hardest days.

**Slow cooker or instant pot:** If she has access to one, a slow cooker is transformative for postpartum nutrition. She can prepare a meal in five minutes in the morning and have a nutritious dinner ready by evening with no further effort.

**Lower the bar on hard days:** On days when sleep deprivation is severe, the baby is unsettled, and cooking is impossible, the goal is simply to eat enough calories from whatever is available. A bowl of cereal with full-fat milk, a banana, and a handful of nuts is not a failure — it is adequate nutrition on a hard day. Perfection is the enemy of good enough, and good enough is entirely sufficient.

---

## Nutrition Across the Programme Phases

### Phase 1 — Weeks 1 and 2
Focus is on establishing the eating pattern and ensuring adequate caloric intake. Many women undereat in the early postpartum weeks due to fatigue, overwhelm, and the mistaken belief that they should be "watching what they eat." Gently challenge this if you observe it. Prioritise protein at every meal, hydration, and the evening snack.

### Phase 2 — Weeks 3 to 6
As activity increases, ensure she is not compensating by eating less. The addition of exercise increases caloric needs. Watch for signs of undereating — excessive fatigue, reduced milk supply, poor exercise recovery, mood deterioration. If she reports any of these, the first question is always whether she is eating enough.

Post-exercise nutrition becomes more important as session intensity increases. By this point she should have a well-established eating pattern that supports her activity level and milk production. # Strength Progression Addendum
### Integrated into the 12-Week Postpartum Return Programme

---

## Trainer Notes on Strength Programming for This Client

Before outlining the progression, establish the following principles clearly in your own programming mindset.

**This is not a standard strength programme with a postpartum modification.** It is a postpartum programme with strength work carefully layered in. The distinction matters because it changes how you respond to setbacks. In a standard strength programme, missing a progression is a programming problem. Here, it may be a healing signal. The hierarchy is always: symptoms first, programme second.

**The load progression model here is conservative by design.** Research on return to loading after C-section consistently shows that the abdominal fascia — specifically the linea alba — is not fully remodelled until at least six to twelve months postpartum. This does not mean she cannot load. It means load must be introduced gradually enough that the tissue can adapt without being overwhelmed. The goal across twelve weeks is to build the foundation so that she can train with meaningful load safely from week thirteen onwards, not to maximise load within the twelve weeks themselves.

**Equipment progression assumes minimal home equipment.** The programme begins with bodyweight only, as specified. Resistance bands are introduced first as they are inexpensive, compact, and provide accommodating resistance — meaning the load is lower at the most vulnerable point of the range of motion. Light dumbbells or a single kettlebell are introduced in Phase 3 and 4. If she does not have these, bodyweight progressions are provided as alternatives throughout.

**The five signals that mean stop and reassess before adding load:**
- Visible coning or doming along the midline during any exercise
- Urinary leaking during or after exercise
- Pelvic heaviness or a sensation of something falling out
- Pain at the scar site during or after exercise
- Joint pain, particularly in the pelvis, hips, or wrists — relaxin remains elevated during breastfeeding and joint laxity is a real consideration

If any of these occur, do not progress load. Regress to the previous week's loading, address the symptom, and refer to pelvic floor physiotherapist if symptoms persist beyond one session.

| Phase 2 — Weeks 3–4 | Bodyweight only | Movement patterns established before load |

# PHASE 1 STRENGTH NOTES
## Weeks 1–2 — No External Load

There is no strength work in the traditional sense during Phase 1, and this is correct. However, frame this for your client not as an absence of training but as the most important strength work she will do in the entire programme. The neuromuscular reconnection happening in these two weeks — the re-establishment of the breath-pelvic floor-deep core relationship — is the literal foundation upon which all subsequent loading sits. A woman who skips this phase and goes straight to goblet squats will have a weaker foundation at week twelve than one who spent two weeks doing nothing but breathing and pelvic floor work.

**The strength work in Phase 1 is:**
- Diaphragmatic breathing under control
- Pelvic floor lift and release with full conscious awareness
- Transversus abdominis gentle activation on the exhale
- Walking as progressive load on the postural system

That is enough. Resist any urge — yours or hers — to add more.

---
---

# PHASE 2 STRENGTH PROGRESSION
## Weeks 3–6 — Bodyweight to Band Loading

---

## Weeks 3–4 — Establishing Bodyweight Patterns

The strength focus in weeks three and four is **movement quality under bodyweight load with correct intra-abdominal pressure management.** Every exercise is an opportunity to practise the exhale-on-effort breathing pattern that will govern all loaded work going forward. If she cannot maintain this pattern under bodyweight, she is not ready for external load.

### The Exhale-on-Effort Rule
Establish this as a non-negotiable from week three onwards. On every exercise, she exhales during the effort phase — the push, the pull, the lift, the stand — and inhales during the return or lowering phase. This coordinates the diaphragm and pelvic floor as a pressure management system and protects the healing linea alba from excessive intra-abdominal pressure spikes. It should become automatic by the end of Phase 2.

---

### Week 3 — Strength Session Structure

**Session A — Posterior Chain and Core**

*Glute bridge — 3 sets of 10*
Tempo: 2 seconds up, 2-second hold at top, 3 seconds down.
Cue: Exhale as hips rise, inhale as they lower. Feel the glutes engage, not the lower back. The spine stays neutral throughout — no hyperextension at the top.
Progression marker: She can perform all 30 repetitions with consistent tempo, neutral spine, and no breath holding before progressing.

*Heel slides — 3 sets of 8 per side*
Tempo: Slow and controlled throughout.
Cue: Exhale as the leg extends, inhale as it returns. The lower back must not arch away from the mat as the leg extends. If it does, reduce range of motion.
Progression marker: Full range with neutral spine and no doming.

*Four-point opposite arm and leg reach — 3 sets of 8 per side*
Tempo: 3-second hold at full extension.
Cue: Exhale as the arm and leg extend, inhale as they return. The pelvis stays level — place a folded towel on her lower back and ask her to keep it from falling as a feedback tool.
Progression marker: 3-second hold with level pelvis and no rotation in the ribcage or hips.

*Clamshell — 3 sets of 12 per side*
Tempo: 2 seconds open, 1-second hold, 3 seconds close.
Cue: The pelvis does not roll backward as the knee opens. If it does, reduce range of motion.
Progression marker: Full range with pelvis completely still.

**Session B — Upper Body and Posture**

*Wall push-up — 3 sets of 10*
Tempo: 3 seconds down, 1-second pause at the wall, 2 seconds push.
Cue: Exhale on the push. Body stays in a straight line from head to heel — no sagging hips or raised bottom. This is a plank with a push, not just an arm exercise.
Progression marker: All 30 repetitions with straight body line and consistent tempo.

*Prone Y-T-W — 2 sets of 8 each shape*
Tempo: 2-second lift, 3-second hold, controlled lower.
Cue: Squeeze the shoulder blades together and down before lifting the arms. The neck stays long — forehead rests on a folded towel.
Progression marker: All positions held for 3 seconds with no neck tension.

*Thoracic rotation in side-lying — 2 sets of 10 per side*
Tempo: Slow and breath-led — the rotation follows the exhale.
Cue: The lower body stays completely still. The rotation comes from the thoracic spine, not the lumbar spine.

**Session C — Full Body Bodyweight**

*Supported squat — 3 sets of 12*
Holding a door frame or sturdy chair back.
Tempo: 3 seconds down, 1-second pause at bottom, 2 seconds up.
Cue: Exhale on the way up. Chest stays tall. Knees track over the second toe. Heels stay flat.
Progression marker: Comfortable full depth with consistent tempo before removing support.

*Standing hip hinge — 3 sets of 10*
Tempo: 3 seconds hinge forward, 2 seconds return.
Cue: Hinge from the hips, not the waist. Spine stays long and neutral. Hands slide down the thighs as a guide. Feel the hamstrings load, not the lower back.
Progression marker: Consistent neutral spine throughout full range.

*Step-up — 3 sets of 10 per side*
Using the bottom stair.
Tempo: Controlled step up and controlled step down.
Cue: Exhale as she steps up. Drive through the heel of the working foot. The knee of the working leg tracks over the second toe.
Progression marker: No lateral hip drop, consistent tempo, no pushing off the back foot.

---

### Week 4 — Bodyweight Progression

In week four, progress the following variables. Do not progress all exercises simultaneously — choose the exercises where she has clearly met the progression marker.

**Glute bridge:** Progress to a **3-second hold** at the top. If this is comfortable across all three sets, introduce the **single-leg glute bridge** — one foot flat, the other leg extended with the knee straight. Begin with 3 sets of 6 per side and build from there. This is a significant progression and should only be introduced if the double-leg version is completely symptom-free.

**Four-point reach:** Increase hold to **5 seconds**. Add a slow **3-count return** — she does not drop the arm and leg back to the mat but controls the descent.

**Wall push-up:** Progress to **incline push-up** using the sofa or a low table. The lower the surface, the greater the load. Begin with the highest available surface and work down over subsequent weeks.

**Supported squat:** Remove the support for the last set only. If this is comfortable, remove support for all sets in week five.

**Hip hinge:** Add a **3-second pause** at the bottom of the hinge, feeling the hamstring load before returning. This increases time under tension without adding external load.

---

## Weeks 5–6 — Resistance Band Introduction

### Equipment Needed
- One **loop resistance band** — light to medium resistance (approximately 10–20kg resistance rating). Fabric bands are more comfortable than latex for postpartum use as they do not roll or pinch.
- One **long resistance band** — light resistance for upper body work.

If she does not have bands, all exercises below have a bodyweight alternative listed.

### Why Bands Before Dumbbells

Resistance bands provide **accommodating resistance** — the load increases as the band stretches, meaning it is lightest at the most vulnerable point of the range of motion (typically the bottom of a squat or the start of a pull) and heaviest at the strongest point. This is mechanically appropriate for a healing postpartum body. Bands also require no grip strength, which is relevant as relaxin-related joint laxity can affect wrist and hand comfort with dumbbells.

---

### Week 5 — Band Integration

**Add to Session A:**

*Banded glute bridge — 3 sets of 12*
Place the loop band just above the knees. Perform the glute bridge as established, now pressing the knees outward against the band throughout. This adds hip abductor activation and increases glute recruitment without loading the spine or abdomen.
Cue: The knees press out against the band on the way up and stay pressed out at the top. Do not let the knees cave inward on the way down.
Load: Light band. If she cannot maintain knee position throughout, the band is too heavy.

*Banded clamshell — 3 sets of 15 per side*
Loop band just above the knees. Same movement as established, now against band resistance.
Cue: Slow and controlled. The band should provide noticeable resistance but not so much that the pelvis rolls.

*Banded hip abduction standing — 3 sets of 12 per side*
Loop band just above the ankles. Standing, holding a wall for balance, she lifts one leg directly out to the side to hip height and returns slowly.
Tempo: 2 seconds out, 2-second hold, 3 seconds return.
Cue: The standing leg stays soft — do not lock the knee. The pelvis stays level — no lateral tilt as the leg lifts.
Bodyweight alternative: Same movement without band, focusing on slow tempo and pelvic stability.

**Add to Session B:**

*Banded pull-apart — 3 sets of 12*
Holding the long band with both hands at shoulder width, arms extended in front at shoulder height, she pulls the band apart until her arms are wide, squeezing the shoulder blades together, then returns slowly.
Tempo: 2 seconds pull, 2-second hold, 3 seconds return.
Cue: Keep the arms at shoulder height throughout. The movement comes from the shoulder blades, not the elbows bending.
Bodyweight alternative: Prone Y-T-W with increased hold time.

*Banded row in seated — 3 sets of 12*
Sitting on the mat with legs extended, loop the long band around both feet. Hold one end in each hand. She rows both hands toward her lower ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades together, then returns with control.
Tempo: 2 seconds pull, 2-second hold, 3 seconds return.
Cue: Exhale on the pull. Sit tall — do not round the lower back as the hands return forward.
Bodyweight alternative: Four-point kneeling row simulation as established.

**Add to Session C:**

*Banded squat — 3 sets of 12*
Loop band just above the knees. Perform the now-unassisted squat with the band providing resistance to knee cave.
Cue: Press the knees outward against the band throughout the entire movement. Exhale on the way up.
Note: The band here is a cue tool as much as a resistance tool — it teaches correct knee tracking under load.

---

### Week 6 — Band Loading Increase and New Patterns

**Progress existing band exercises:**
- Banded glute bridge: Progress to **single-leg banded glute bridge** — band above the knees, one foot flat, one leg extended. 3 sets of 8 per side.
- Banded pull-apart: Increase to 15 repetitions or move to a medium resistance band.
- Banded row: Increase to 15 repetitions.

**Add new exercises:**

*Banded deadlift pattern — 3 sets of 10*
Stand on the centre of the long band, holding one end in each hand. Perform the hip hinge pattern established in week three, now with the band providing resistance as she returns to standing.
Tempo: 3 seconds hinge down, 2 seconds stand up.
Cue: Exhale as she stands. The band pulls her forward — she resists this by keeping the spine long and the hips driving forward. This is the first loaded hip hinge and the direct precursor to the dumbbell Romanian deadlift in Phase 3.
Bodyweight alternative: Hip hinge with 5-second pause at the bottom.

*Banded lateral walk — 2 sets of 12 steps each direction*
Loop band just above the ankles. Standing with feet hip-width apart and a slight bend in the knees, she steps sideways — maintaining the band tension throughout — for twelve steps in one direction, then twelve back.
Cue: Keep the chest tall and the hips level. Do not let the feet come together completely between steps — maintain tension in the band throughout.

*Banded glute kickback on all fours — 3 sets of 12 per side*
On hands and knees, loop band around one foot and anchor the other end under the opposite hand. She extends the banded leg straight back to hip height and returns.
Tempo: 2 seconds back, 2-second hold, 3 seconds return.
Cue: The spine stays neutral — no arching as the leg extends. The pelvis stays level.

---

### Phase 2 Strength Summary — End of Week 6

By the end of week six she should have established the following strength foundations. She can perform a full bodyweight squat with correct breathing and no symptoms. She can perform a single-leg glute bridge with control. She can perform a hip hinge pattern under band resistance. She has basic upper body pulling and pushing strength through bands and bodyweight. She understands and consistently applies the exhale-on-effort principle. She is ready for dumbbell loading.

# PHASE 3 STRENGTH PROGRESSION
## Weeks 7–10 — Dumbbell and Kettlebell Introduction

---

## Dumbbell Introduction Principles

Introduce dumbbells conservatively. The first session with dumbbells should feel almost too easy — this is correct. The purpose of the first week with any new implement is to learn how to manage the load, not to be challenged by it. Challenge comes in subsequent weeks.

**Starting weights:** 2–4kg dumbbells for upper body exercises. 4–6kg for lower body exercises where the load is distributed across larger muscle groups. These numbers will feel light to a woman who trained before pregnancy. That is appropriate. She is not the same body she was before pregnancy, and the goal is not to return to previous loads but to build new, better-supported strength.

**Grip and wrist awareness:** Relaxin remains elevated during breastfeeding and can cause wrist laxity and discomfort. If she reports wrist pain with dumbbell work, check her grip — she should hold dumbbells with a neutral wrist, not a flexed or extended one. Wrist wraps are a reasonable short-term solution if discomfort persists.

---

### Week 7 — Dumbbell Introduction

**Session A — Lower Body Strength**

*Goblet squat — 3 sets of 10 @ 4kg*
Hold one dumbbell vertically at the chest with both hands. Perform the squat as established, now with the counterbalance of the dumbbell allowing a more upright torso.
Tempo: 3 seconds down, 1-second pause at bottom, 2 seconds up.
Cue: Exhale on the way up. The dumbbell stays close to the chest — do not let it pull her forward. Press the knees out as established with the band.
Progression: Increase load by 1–2kg when she can complete all sets with consistent tempo and no symptoms.

*Romanian deadlift — 3 sets of 10 @ 4kg each hand*
Hold one dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging in front of the thighs. Hinge from the hips as established, allowing the dumbbells to travel down the front of the legs, then drive the hips forward to return to standing.
Tempo: 3 seconds down, 2 seconds up.
Cue: Exhale on the way up. The dumbbells stay close to the legs throughout — they should almost brush the shins. Feel the hamstrings load, not the lower back. If the lower back rounds, reduce range of motion.
Progression: Increase load by 1–2kg per hand when form is consistent across all sets.

*Single-leg glute bridge — 3 sets of 10 per side*
Bodyweight only for now — the single-leg version is sufficient challenge without adding load.
Progress to adding a dumbbell across the hip in week nine.

*Banded lateral walk — 2 sets of 15 steps each direction*
Continuing from Phase 2.

**Session B — Upper Body Strength**

*Dumbbell floor press — 3 sets of 10 @ 3kg each hand*
Lying on her back, knees bent, one dumbbell in each hand at chest height with elbows at approximately 45 degrees from the body. She presses the dumbbells up until the arms are extended, then lowers with control.
Tempo: 3 seconds down, 1-second pause at chest, 2 seconds press.
Cue: Exhale on the press. The lower back stays in neutral — do not arch to press. This is the precursor to a bench press and is appropriate at this stage because the floor limits the range of motion, protecting the shoulder at the bottom.
Progression: Increase load by 1kg per hand when all sets are completed with consistent tempo.

*Dumbbell bent-over row — 3 sets of 10 per side @ 4kg*
Hinge forward from the hips to approximately 45 degrees, one dumbbell in one hand, the other hand resting on the thigh for support. She rows the dumbbell to her lower ribs, squeezing the shoulder blade, then lowers with control.
Tempo: 2 seconds up, 2-second hold, 3 seconds down.
Cue: Exhale on the row. The elbow stays close to the body. The spine stays neutral throughout — do not rotate the torso to lift the weight.
Progression: Increase load by 1–2kg when form is consistent.

*Dumbbell lateral raise — 3 sets of 12 @ 2kg*
Standing, one dumbbell in each hand at the sides. She raises both arms out to the sides to shoulder height and lowers slowly.
Tempo: 2 seconds up, 2-second hold, 3 seconds down.
Cue: Exhale on the raise. Slight bend in the elbows throughout. Do not shrug the shoulders — keep them down and back.
Note: 2kg will feel very light. This is correct — the lateral raise is a small muscle exercise and the rotator cuff is vulnerable to overload. Build slowly.

*Dumbbell bicep curl — 3 sets of 12 @ 3kg*
Standing, one dumbbell in each hand. Alternate curls, keeping the elbows tucked to the sides.
Cue: Exhale on the curl. Do not swing the body to lift the weight. This is included not just for aesthetics but because carrying a baby is a significant bicep and forearm demand — building this strength has direct functional relevance.

**Session C — Full Body Strength**

*Superset 1 — 3 rounds, 60 seconds rest between rounds:*
- Goblet squat × 10 @ 4kg
- Dumbbell bent-over row × 10 per side @ 4kg

*Superset 2 — 3 rounds:*
- Romanian deadlift × 10 @ 4kg each hand
- Dumbbell floor press × 10 @ 3kg each hand

*Superset 3 — 3 rounds:*
- Reverse lunge × 10 per side bodyweight
- Banded pull-apart × 12

*Finisher:*
- Dead bug × 6 per side
- Banded glute bridge × 15

**Load increases this week:**
- Goblet squat: Progress to 6kg if week 7 was comfortable.
- Romanian deadlift: Progress to 5–6kg per hand.
- Bent-over row: Progress to 5–6kg.
- Floor press: Progress to 4kg per hand.

**New exercises introduced:**

*Dumbbell reverse lunge — 3 sets of 10 per side @ 3kg each hand*
Holding one dumbbell in each hand at the sides, she performs the reverse lunge as established. The dumbbells add load without changing the movement pattern.

Standing, one dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing forward. She presses both dumbbells overhead until the arms are extended, then lowers with control.

# Core Restoration Guide
### When and How to Reintroduce Abdominal Training Post C-Section

---

## The Most Important Reframe You Will Do With This Client

Before answering the question of when, address the question of **what she actually means** when she says she wants her core back. In most cases, a postpartum woman saying this means one or more of the following things. She wants her abdomen to look flatter. She wants to feel strong through her middle again. She wants to stop feeling like her torso is disconnected from her legs. She wants to feel like herself again.

All of these are valid. But none of them are solved by crunches.

The core she had before pregnancy was built on top of an intact abdominal wall, a well-functioning pelvic floor, and a linea alba under normal tension. She now has a surgically repaired uterus, a healing scar through multiple abdominal layers, potential changes to linea alba width and tension, a pelvic floor that has been under nine months of increased load, and hormonal changes that affect connective tissue stiffness throughout her body. The path back to a strong, functional, visible core runs directly through the deep system — not through surface-level abdominal exercises.

**The honest conversation to have with her:**

Tell her that the exercises that will give her her core back are not the ones she is probably imagining. Tell her that crunches and sit-ups, introduced too early or without the deep system foundation in place, can actually make the appearance of her abdomen worse by increasing intra-abdominal pressure on a linea alba that is not yet ready to manage it. Tell her that the work she has already been doing — the breathing, the pelvic floor reconnection, the dead bugs, the loaded hip hinges — is core work. It is the most important core work she will ever do. And tell her that if she is patient and systematic, she will have a stronger, more functional core at month six than she had before pregnancy.

That is not a consolation prize. That is the truth.

---

## Understanding What "Core" Actually Means

The core is not the rectus abdominis — the six-pack muscle. The core is a canister. It has a roof, which is the diaphragm. It has a floor, which is the pelvic floor. It has a front and sides, which are the transversus abdominis and internal obliques. And it has a back, which is the multifidus and erector spinae. All four walls of this canister must work together to manage intra-abdominal pressure during movement and load.

A C-section cuts through the front wall of this canister. The rectus abdominis itself is not cut — it is separated at the midline and moved aside — but the fascia that connects it to the deeper layers is disrupted, and the transversus abdominis and its fascial connections are directly incised. This means the canister has a structural compromise that must be respected during rehabilitation.

**The progression of core restoration therefore follows this sequence:**

1. Restore the roof — diaphragmatic breathing mechanics
2. Restore the floor — pelvic floor reconnection and coordination
3. Restore the deep front wall — transversus abdominis activation
4. Restore the back wall — multifidus and erector spinae through loaded movement
5. Restore the obliques — rotational and anti-rotational control
6. Restore the rectus abdominis — direct abdominal loading

This programme has been following exactly this sequence. By the time direct abdominal work is introduced, steps one through five will already be well established.

---

## The Diastasis Recti Assessment — Do This Before Any Direct Ab Work

Diastasis recti — the separation of the rectus abdominis at the linea alba — affects approximately 100% of women at full term pregnancy to some degree, and a significant proportion retain clinically relevant separation postpartum. C-section does not cause diastasis but does not prevent it either, and the surgical disruption of the fascial layers makes assessment particularly important before loading the rectus abdominis directly.

**You are not qualified to diagnose diastasis recti.** A pelvic floor physiotherapist assesses this with ultrasound or manual palpation and evaluates not just the width of the gap but the tension and function of the linea alba — which is the more clinically relevant factor. A wide gap with good tension may be more functional than a narrow gap with poor tension.

**However, you can perform a basic screening check** to determine whether direct abdominal loading is appropriate or whether referral is needed first.

### Basic Diastasis Screen

Have her lie on her back with knees bent. Ask her to place her fingertips horizontally across her midline at the navel. She then performs a very small head lift — just lifting the head off the mat, not a crunch. You or she observes and feels for:

- **Width:** How many fingers fit in the gap at the midline? One to two fingers is generally considered within normal range. Two to three fingers warrants monitoring. More than three fingers warrants physiotherapy referral before progressing to direct abdominal loading.
- **Depth:** Do the fingers sink deeply into the gap, or is there resistance? Deep sinking with little resistance indicates poor linea alba tension regardless of width.
- **Coning or doming:** Does the midline rise up into a ridge or cone shape? This indicates the linea alba is being pushed outward by intra-abdominal pressure rather than managing it — a sign that the load is too great.

**Perform this screen at the six-week check-in and again before introducing each new level of abdominal loading.**

If she has not seen a pelvic floor physiotherapist by the time you are ready to introduce direct abdominal work, make this a condition of progression. It is not optional at this stage.
